title: Dominant species, widespread and abundant, produce the most varieties

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Dominant species, widespread and abundant, produce the most varieties

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The dominant species, those that range widely over the world, are most diffused in their own country and are most numerous in individuals, most often produce well-marked varieties.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Hence it is the most flourishing, or, as they may be called, the dominant species,—those which range widely over the world, are the most diffused in their own country, and are the most numerous in individuals,—which oftenest produce well-marked varieties, or, as I consider them, incipient species.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter II, “Variation under Nature”; section “Wide ranging, much diffused, and common species vary most”. Scope: plants in regional floras

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch02-07: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.79

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Global occurrence and plant taxonomic resources directly support a broad modern replication. Bias-aware hierarchical models can discriminate the predicted association, although abundance remains a proxy.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Model the number or probability of recognized infraspecific varieties as a function of range size, occupancy and abundance across regional floras, controlling sampling and taxonomy. Positive associations for all three dominance measures support the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Abundance is poorly estimated by opportunistic occurrences.

Sampling effort inflates both range and recorded varieties.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.88
analysis feasibility: 0.76
data adequacy: 0.68
operationalizability: 0.86
discriminating power: 0.74

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Range, plot, and flora databases contain the dominance variables and at least partial variety counts for plants, which is the stated scope. The classic sampling bias, that common plants attract more taxonomic attention, is large enough that an uncorrected regression would not discriminate the biological claim. A careful subset analysis is feasible; a global, bias-resistant one is not sitting ready to run.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Regress the number of well-marked varieties per species on geographic range, local occupancy, and abundance, within regional floras, with sampling effort as a covariate. A positive partial association for wide, common species would support the pattern; no association after effort is controlled would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Widespread species are collected and split more often, which manufactures varieties.

Abundance, range, and 'variety' rank are complete together only for some regional floras.

Darwin's dominance criteria (world range, local diffusion, and numbers) are only partly observed in the same records.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.46
analysis feasibility: 0.58
operationalizability: 0.78
data existence: 0.68
data adequacy: 0.5
